text:
SCIENCE COMMUNICATION

Science Writer (Community Contributor)
The Life Raft Group (patient advocacy & research for rare cancers such as GIST and liposarcoma) 2026 (Present)


Highlights from the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) Annual Meeting Recap Webinar
Levies on an ever-growing insight into gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs), a class of soft tissue sarcomas, to translate complex biomedical literature into accessible prose for newly diagnosed patients and their family members.
Authors content from the intersection of technical rigor and empathy to encourage research participation and empower patients with a greater understanding of their condition.
Acts as a bridge between cancer biologists, medical professionals, and patient networks to transmit research discoveries from their source to those most directly affected, ensuring audience accessibility without compromising accuracy.




Science Writer and Content Developer
Slingshot Biosciences 2022


Led content development for the launch of flow cytometry and synthetic cell biology reagents, producing educational writing, scientific figures, application notes, and articles that communicated product value to both scientific and commercial audiences.
Collaborated cross-functionally with the R&D team, leveraging proficiency in data interpretation and scientific literature review to distill experimental findings into nuanced, plain-language insights that directly informed and strengthened messaging.

title: CURRICULUM VITAE
text:
RESEARCH EXPERIENCE

Molecular Biology Research Associate
University of Colorado, Anschutz Medical Campus 2020 – 2021


Contributed to research in neuronal cells validating and examining active oligonucleotide sequences within 3′ UTRs found to be sufficient and necessary to drive localization of their transcripts to neurites. This established the groundwork for identification of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) such as Unk (Unkempt), as associated with relevant sequence elements and required for efficient localization of the studied transcripts to neurites.
Built upon a workflow for smFISH (Fluorescence in situ hybridization) image data capture and analysis, improving the accuracy and completeness of spacial visualization of relevant RNAs in cells with complex, elongated morphology.
Communicated research findings through presentations and written reports for both scientific peers and a broader community of molecular biologists, translating technical results into clear, structured narratives.




Microbiology Research Technician II
Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) Division of Infectious Diseases 2017 – 2019


Created a comprehensive epidemiological database by consolidating and analyzing pertinent information for approximately 800 cholera patients and their 1700 plus household contacts collected over the course of two decades.
Contributed to an ongoing systems serology-based initiative to identify novel humoral correlates of protection against infection with Vibrio cholerae by providing expertise in high throughput analysis of results and by performing a variety of assays such as Ig Luminex, ELISA, Antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis assays, and others that measure functional activity of antibodies in convalescent Cholera-patient serum.
Conducted serosurveillance of cholera endemic areas such as several sites in Haiti, and Dhaka, Bangladesh by conducting high-throughput sample evaluation by real time qPCR, multiplex PCR, ELISA and vibriocidal titer assays.
Mentored and instructed research students, as well as guided incoming research technicians throughout their initial training.
Devised new protocols, upgraded existing methods, and authored highly detailed SOPs.
Managed working order of the lab by procuring necessary reagents and supplies, maintaining and purchasing new equipment, and cataloging samples received by the lab.

Diversity of Klebsiella Surface Antigens O and K
text:
Many Klebsiella species can be found in low numbers in a healthy human microbiome;1,2 still, opportunistic agents within the genus, including members of the Klebsiella pneumoniae species complex, Klebsiella oxytoca, and several others, represent long-standing threats to immunocompromised and otherwise vulnerable individuals.4 These conditional pathogens are causative agents of a range of healthcare-associated infections, including nosocomial pneumonia, catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs), surgical site and wound abscesses, and fatal sepsis.3,4







In recent years, emerging hyper-virulent (hvKp) and multi-drug resistant (MDR/cKp) Klebsiella strains have also begun to affect immunocompetent individuals, and now pose a mounting worldwide health concern.1-8 These infectious Klebsiella species possess an arsenal of virulence factors that contribute to pathogenicity and assist in evasion of the host immune response.2,3-5
Klebsiella K antigens (capsular polysaccharides) are a diverse group of surface molecules containing 77-79 serologically-characterized structural variations.5 Broadly, K antigens help protect the bacteria from the host immune response at multiple levels, helping it to evade cell-mediated immunity and block innate immune signaling cascades.4,7 The K antigen group has a hand in reducing engulfment of the bacteria by epithelial cells, avoiding phagocytosis by macrophages and neutrophils, interrupting NF-kB signaling, and triggering cell death and cytotoxicity in host cells.4,6 In hvKp strains specifically, key K antigens, such as K1 and K2 (Figures 1 and 2), help the opportunistic pathogen evade clearance by the host by conferring increased resistance against two of these facets of the immune response: complement-mediated killing and phagocytosis.6







The O-specific polysaccharides (OPS), or O antigens, are a group containing around 9-13 structural variations, although O1, O2, and O3 (Figure 2) are identified in about 80% of infections.5 In tandem with CPS, O-specific polysaccharides help counter the host immune response by suppressing TLR-signaling and facilitating resistance to complement-mediated killing through interference with C3b deposition.6,7 The O1 variant is often seen in hvKp infections along with K1 and K2; at present, O1, O2, O3, and O5 are represented across emerging MDR/cKp strains.6 Altogether, the structure of these factors varies meaningfully across distinct strains, contributing in part to the rapidly developing pathologies seen in MDR, hvKp, and convergent (MDR-hvKp) species.6-8
Over the past two decades, multi-drug resistance has been increasingly observed as a regular and concerning feature of severe human infection by opportunistic and hyper-virulent Klebsiella species.5,6 The spread of drug resistance forebodes an eventual narrowing of treatment options for Klebsiella infection, while, in parallel, an increase in hyper-virulence abets a concurrent widening of the susceptible population.8 The role of surface antigenic variation in individuating MDR and HV-specific pathology warrants further characterization of these rapidly-evolving virulence factors.4,7,8 Exploration of novel therapeutic agents and vaccines targeting these antigens denotes a promising strategy to preempt this rising global health threat.6,8
